messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Curriculum Designer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 33

He is thirty years old, African, single, and works as a curriculum designer for a nonprofit educational organization. His apartment is neat, almost sterile—a space he keeps ordered so nothing can surprise him. He comes to therapy because his supervisor suggested it after noticing that he flinches whenever a coworker walks up behind his desk. He does not think he needs therapy, but he also knows he has not slept through the night in over a year.

The trauma began two years ago, when he was living with a woman he had been with for almost three years. She was charismatic, successful, and intensely jealous. At first her jealousy felt flattering, a sign of devotion. But the first slap came six months in, after a party where he spoke to a female colleague for too long. She apologized immediately, crying, promising it would never happen again. He believed her. He loved her.

The physical abuse escalated slowly—shoves, pinches, a thrown phone, a punch to his ribs that left a bruise he covered with gym excuses. He started walking on eggshells. He changed how he dressed, whom he texted, how long he stayed at work. He stopped seeing his friends. At the time he told himself he was being a good partner. He told himself she was under a lot of stress. He rationalized every incident until the night she hit him in the face with a glass bottle, splitting his eyebrow open. He sat in the emergency room and told the doctor he had tripped. That was the last time he saw her. But she did not leave him—he left her, in the middle of the night, with only a backpack and his laptop.

Now, he designs curricula for middle-school social studies. He is good at it—he writes lesson plans that guide students through complex historical topics with clear, predictable steps. He likes the structure. He avoids units on conflict, power dynamics, or personal relationships. When he has to include content about domestic violence for a health class module, he delegates that section to a colleague without explaining why. His desk is arranged so that his back is to the wall and he can see the door. He does not tolerate loud noises. A door slamming in the hallway makes his heart pound and his hands go cold.

He has not dated since the breakup. He deleted all his dating apps. When a friendly barista smiles at him, he feels a cold dread instead of warmth. He tells himself he is protecting others from his baggage, but deep down he knows he is protecting himself from being hurt again. He avoids crowded places, especially at night. He changed his commute to a longer route that passes fewer bars and restaurants where couples might be laughing. At home he keeps the television on low volume, checking the locks three times before bed.

His sleep is fractured. He wakes up at least twice a night, often from a dream in which he is pinned down, unable to move or shout. In the dream her face is not her face—it is an abstract, monstrous shadow. He lies awake afterward, listening to the silence, waiting for something to break. On workdays he functions on four or five hours of sleep, surviving on caffeine and willpower.

He is irritable with colleagues over small things—a misplaced file, a last-minute meeting request—and then he apologizes excessively, fearing he has made someone angry. He has trouble concentrating on reading, needing to re-read paragraphs multiple times. His PCL-5 score of 33 reflects the weight he carries: the hypervigilance, the avoidance, the numbing, the negative beliefs about himself. He believes he should have been stronger, should have left earlier, should have seen the signs. He believes that loving someone means being vulnerable, and vulnerability is now synonymous with danger.

He comes to therapy because his supervisor said it was a good idea. He sits on the edge of the chair, not fully relaxed. He speaks quietly, measuring his words. He does not know if talking will help. But he is tired of checking every corner, tired of flinching at kindness, tired of living in a world where the safest place is alone.
